title: Exam study path

bites.title: The basics everything else builds on
bites.html: Lecture 2 (Intro to ecology) plus section 1 of the glossary, Ecology in the Anthropocene. Short, but the exam loves the definitions and the Darwin vs Wallace story.

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Ecology = how organisms interact with each other and their physical environment: why they live where they do, in the numbers they do.
  • The word comes from Greek oîkos (house) + logía (study of).
  • Natural selection needs three things: variation in traits, differential reproduction and heredity.

bites.q: Which is the best definition of ecology?
options: The science of how organisms interact with each other and with their physical environment
The study of how traits are inherited from parents
The classification and naming of species
bites.why: Glossary 1a: ecology asks why organisms are distributed and abundant as they are, shaped by biotic and abiotic processes.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Darwin saw competition between individuals as the driving force of selection, Wallace saw the environment.
  • Habitat is where an organism lives; the niche is its role and requirements.
  • Fundamental niche = what physiology allows; realized niche = what it actually occupies with competitors and predators around.

bites.q: What happened on 1 July 1858?
options: A joint reading of Wallace's essay and Darwin's writings at the Linnean Society
Darwin published On the Origin of Species
bites.why: Darwin received Wallace's Ternate essay on 18 June 1858; the joint Linnean reading followed on 1 July. The Origin came out in 1859.

bites.q: According to the lecture, what did Wallace see as the main driving force of selection?
bites.why: Darwin stressed competition between individuals; Wallace stressed the environment.

bites.title: Patterns in body size, shape and colour
bites.html: The end of Lecture 2 (ecogeographical rules) and the Lecture 3 example talk on the island rule, plus how a scientific paper is built. Glossary section 6 i–l.

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Bergmann's rule: larger bodies in colder climates.
  • Allen's rule: shorter extremities in cold regions.
  • Gloger's rule: darker pigmentation in warm, humid areas.

bites.q: Which rule says animals in colder climates tend to have larger bodies?
bites.why: Bergmann: larger bodies in colder climates.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Island rule (Foster's rule): small species get bigger (gigantism), large species get smaller (dwarfism) on islands.
  • A meta-analysis statistically combines results of many studies; for the island rule, author groups disagree, so the verdict is: it generally holds, but depends on context and lineage, and methods matter.
  • Abstract → Introduction (what is known), Methods (data & stats), Results, Discussion (interpretation).

bites.q: Which rule says animals in cold regions have shorter extremities (ears, legs)?
bites.why: Allen: shorter extremities in cold regions.

bites.q: Which rule links darker pigmentation to warm, humid areas?
bites.why: Gloger: darker colour in warm, humid areas.

bites.title: Does the fast–slow continuum capture life-history variation?
bites.html: Group 1's question: does the fast–slow continuum capture life-history variation across taxa, or do we need several axes? Classic paper Stearns (1977), recent paper Stott et al. (2024), 'Life histories are not just fast or slow'.

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Life-history traits: growth, age and size at maturity, number and size of offspring, lifespan.
  • Fast = early reproduction, many small offspring, short life, high mortality. Slow = the opposite.
  • The slow–fast continuum is the main axis, defined by the trade-off between time spent on reproduction and development versus survival.

bites.q: Which of these is a life-history trait?
bites.why: Life-history traits concern growth, reproduction and survival: age at maturity, offspring number and size, lifespan.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Pace-of-life syndromes add behaviour and physiology: fast, bold, high-metabolism vs slow, shy, low-metabolism.
  • It works as the dominant axis in tetrapods, and broadly in vascular plants and corals; few studies in invertebrates (except insects).
  • Answer: the fast–slow axis is the main one for some taxa, but multiple axes are needed (e.g. reproductive patterns, stature–recruitment, altricial vs precocial).

bites.q: Which set describes a FAST life history?
options: Early reproduction, many small offspring, short lifespan
Late reproduction, few large offspring, long lifespan
Early reproduction, few large offspring, long lifespan
Late reproduction, many small offspring, short lifespan
bites.why: Fast = early, many, small, short-lived, high mortality.

bites.q: Pace-of-life syndromes add which kinds of traits to life history?
bites.why: E.g. fast-growing, bold, high-metabolism vs slow-growing, shy, low-metabolism.

bites.title: Allee effects: curiosity or fundamental driver?
bites.html: Group 2's question: are Allee effects an ecological curiosity or a fundamental driver of population dynamics? Classic paper Stephens, Sutherland & Freckleton (1999), recent paper Muir, Lajeunesse & Kramer (2024).

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Allee effect: the smaller the population, the lower each individual's chance of surviving or reproducing.
  • Component Allee effect: one fitness component (e.g. pup survival) drops at low density. Demographic: overall growth per individual of the whole population drops.
  • Strong Allee effect: a threshold below which growth is negative and extinction is likely. Weak: growth is slower at low density, but no hard threshold.

bites.q: What is the Allee effect, in one line?
options: Smaller populations mean lower individual survival or reproduction
bites.why: Group 2: the smaller the population, the lower each individual's chance of surviving or reproducing.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Rescue effect: immigrants from other populations prevent or delay local extinction.
  • Mechanisms: mates (sea urchins), safety (island marmots), teamwork (African wild dogs), changing habitat (bark beetles).
  • Group 2's answer: not a curiosity, but a fundamental driver for small, declining and harvested populations, often before we can detect it.

bites.q: A positive relationship between ONE measurable fitness component and density is a…
bites.why: Glossary 3a; e.g. pup survival in African wild dogs.

bites.q: What defines a STRONG Allee effect?
options: A threshold density below which growth is negative
Growth is slower at low density but always positive
It affects only one fitness component
bites.why: Below the threshold, extinction is likely.

bites.title: Does predation grip prey numbers?
bites.html: Group 3's question: top-down control or bottom-up release? The test case is the snowshoe hare cycle in Kluane, Yukon. Classic: Krebs et al. (1995). Recent: Oli et al. (2026).

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Top-down control: consumers (predators) regulate the lower trophic levels.
  • Bottom-up control: resource supply (food, nutrients, plant productivity) sets the higher levels.
  • Predation in the glossary is broad: anything that reduces prey's future survival or reproduction to zero (parasitoids, herbivory, seed predation too).

bites.q: Top-down control means…
options: Consumers mainly regulate the lower trophic levels
Resources mainly regulate the higher levels
bites.why: Glossary 4b.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Trophic cascade: a change at one level ripples down, with alternating rises and falls in biomass.
  • Krebs 1995: food addition AND predator exclusion together gave the biggest effect (~11×), but the decline still came.
  • Oli 2026: 43 years of capture-mark-recapture; declines come from lower survival, mainly before weaning. Verdict: predation matters a lot, but food and demography matter too.

bites.q: Bottom-up control means…
options: Resource supply mainly determines the higher trophic levels
bites.why: Glossary 4c: nutrients and primary production.

bites.q: A trophic cascade is…
options: Effects passing down a food web, with alternating rises and falls in biomass
A single predator eating many prey
bites.why: E.g. more predators → fewer herbivores → more plants.

bites.title: From keystone to rewiring
bites.html: Group 4's question: does food-web complexity build local biodiversity? Their example ecosystem was Lake Nakuru in Kenya. Classic: Paine (1966), food web complexity and species diversity. Recent: Bartley et al. (2019), food web rewiring in a changing world.

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Keystone species: a disproportionately large effect relative to its biomass; removing it can trigger cascades or regime shifts.
  • Interaction strength: how strongly one species affects another's vital rates, abundance or behaviour.
  • Network structure: degree (number of links; hubs), modularity (clusters), motifs (recurring small patterns).

bites.q: A keystone species is one that…
options: Has a disproportionately large effect relative to its biomass or abundance
Is the largest predator by body size
bites.why: Glossary 5a: removing it can cause big shifts, cascades or regime shifts.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Network rewiring: who interacts with whom changes over time, from seasons and range shifts or from humans (land use, invasions, climate).
  • Complexity (many links, alternative prey, varied niches) supports resilience, but complex webs are not automatically stable.
  • Lake Nakuru: cyanobacteria (Spirulina/Arthrospira) → lesser flamingo and soda tilapia → pelicans, cormorants, fish eagle.

bites.q: In a network, a species' degree is…
options: The number of links it has
bites.why: High-degree species act as hubs.

bites.q: Network rewiring is…
options: A change over time in who interacts with whom
Moving species to new places on purpose
Adding fences to keep predators out
bites.why: Links weaken, disappear or form; drivers can be natural or human.

bites.title: Latitudinal gradients in biodiversity: how and why?
bites.html: Your group's topic. Why does biodiversity peak in the tropics and fall toward the poles, and does that hold for every dimension? Classic: Willig, Kaufman & Stevens (2003). Recent: Brodie & Mannion (2023), the hierarchy of factors predicting the LDG.

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Latitudinal diversity gradient (LDG): species richness rises from the poles to the equator, across most groups.
  • Three dimensions: taxonomic (counting species), functional (counting jobs), phylogenetic (measuring shared history).
  • Spatial scales: point, alpha (one community), beta (difference between communities), gamma (many communities).

bites.q: What is the latitudinal diversity gradient?
options: Species richness rises from the poles to the equator
Species richness rises toward the poles
Body size increases toward the poles
Diversity is equal at all latitudes
bites.why: A global, general pattern across most groups.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Causes in order of priority: climate & energy (main driver), habitat area, evolutionary history, biotic factors.
  • Diversification = speciation minus extinction. Tropical conservatism: most lineages evolved in, and stayed adapted to, tropical conditions.
  • Exceptions: parasites, aquatic plants (peak in temperate zones), secondary marine mammals and birds (higher toward poles).

bites.q: According to Group 5 (after Brodie & Mannion), what is the main driver of the LDG?
bites.why: Order: climate & energy → habitat area → evolutionary history → biotic factors.

bites.q: Functional diversity is…
options: The range of traits and ecological roles in a community
The total branch length of a phylogeny
bites.why: 'Counting jobs': diet, body size, dispersal mode.

bites.title: How many species are on Earth, and why is it hard to say?
bites.html: Group 6's question. Classic: Mora et al. (2011), who estimated about 8.7 million species by extrapolating from higher taxa. Recent: Wiens (2023), progress and problems.

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Species concepts: biological (interbreeding, reproductively isolated), morphological (distinct looks), phylogenetic (smallest diagnosable lineage). Different concepts give different counts.
  • The biological species concept (Mayr) fails for asexual organisms and prokaryotes, geographic isolation and hybridisation.
  • Mora et al. 2011: extrapolated from higher taxa (regression) → about 8.75 million species.

bites.q: The biological species concept defines a species as…
options: Interbreeding natural populations reproductively isolated from others
bites.why: Ernst Mayr's concept.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Cryptic diversity: lookalike species lumped under one name (e.g. African savanna vs forest elephant).
  • Wiens 2023 problems: limited DNA data, cryptic diversity, underestimated prokaryotes, and Mora's wrong assumption of stagnation (>700 new genera are described each year).
  • Extrapolation = estimating total richness beyond what was sampled.

bites.q: For which organisms does the biological species concept fail?
bites.why: Also problems with geographic isolation and hybridisation.

bites.q: Roughly how many species did Mora et al. 2011 estimate?
bites.why: 8.75 million, by extrapolating from higher taxa.

bites.title: Are we facing a sixth mass extinction?
bites.html: Group 7's question. Classic: Ceballos et al. (2015), 'Entering the sixth mass extinction'. Recent: Wiens & Saban (2025), 'Questioning the sixth mass extinction'.

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Big Five: periods with ≥75 % species lost: End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian, End-Triassic, End-Cretaceous.
  • Background extinction rate: the natural pace from the fossil record, about 2 E/MSY (extinctions per million species-years).
  • Ceballos 2015 defines mass extinction by rate: modern rates vastly exceed background, even with conservative data.

bites.q: Which list gives the Big Five mass extinctions in order?
options: End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian, End-Triassic, End-Cretaceous
Late Devonian, End-Ordovician, End-Triassic, End-Permian, End-Cretaceous
End-Ordovician, End-Permian, Late Devonian, End-Cretaceous, End-Triassic
bites.why: Glossary 7c.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Wiens & Saban 2025 define it by total loss (75 %), and total loss so far is very low.
  • Extinction debt: species already committed to extinction by past damage, with a time lag of years to centuries.
  • Group 7's verdict: the warning is real (rates are high, humans drive them), but by the 75 % definition we are not there yet. Conservation is the window.

bites.q: What is the background extinction rate used by Ceballos et al.?
bites.why: 0.1–1 E/MSY rounded up to a conservative 2 E/MSY: about 1 extinction per 10,000 species per 100 years.

bites.q: How does Ceballos et al. 2015 define a mass extinction?
options: By how fast species disappear compared with background rates
By the total share of species lost
By the number of new species
bites.why: Rate-based definition.

bites.title: What drives the current biodiversity crisis?
bites.html: Group 8's question. Readings: Jaureguiberry et al. (2022), the direct drivers of recent global biodiversity loss, and Bar-On, Phillips & Milo (2018), the biomass distribution on Earth.

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Biodiversity crisis: global declines in species, populations and ecosystem integrity driven by humans.
  • Direct drivers: measurable pressures that change ecosystems right away (habitat conversion, harvesting, pollution, introductions, greenhouse gases).
  • Indirect drivers: social, economic, demographic, technological and institutional processes behind the direct ones.

bites.q: The biodiversity crisis is…
options: Global declines in species, populations and ecosystem integrity driven by humans
A shortage of new species descriptions
bites.why: Driven by habitat change, exploitation, climate, pollution and invasions.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Jaureguiberry et al. screened 45,162 studies down to 154 for their synthesis, and compared terrestrial, freshwater and marine realms and world regions.
  • Bar-On et al.: biomass measured in gigatons of carbon. Plants ≈ 450 Gt C dominate; animals only ≈ 2 Gt C.
  • Biomass reallocation: livestock (0.1 Gt C) and humans (0.06) far outweigh wild mammals (0.007); wild mammal biomass fell by ~82.5 %.

bites.q: Which is a DIRECT driver of biodiversity loss?
bites.why: Direct = measurable physical, biological or chemical pressures.

bites.q: Which is an INDIRECT driver?
bites.why: Indirect drivers shape the direct pressures in space and time.

bites.title: From services to contributions: valuing nature
bites.html: Group 9's topic. Classic: Costanza et al. (1997), the value of the world's ecosystem services and natural capital. Recent: Díaz et al. (2018), assessing nature's contributions to people.

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Ecosystem services: regulating (climate, floods, water purification), material (crops, fish, timber, medicine), non-material (recreation, beauty, identity).
  • Intrinsic value: nature is worth something in itself. Instrumental: useful for human needs. Relational: value from people's relationships with nature.
  • Costanza 1997 put nature's services at about US$33 trillion a year, about 1.8× the global economy.

bites.q: Flood protection and water purification are which kind of ecosystem service?
bites.why: Regulating: climate regulation, flood protection, water purification.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Díaz 2018 (nature's contributions to people) describes multiple ways of valuing nature, not only money.
  • The two papers overlap: same ground (food, water, regulation), both want nature to count in decisions.
  • Nature-based solutions: conserve, restore or manage ecosystems to solve societal problems while helping biodiversity and people.

bites.q: 'A flower has value simply because it is a living organism.' Which value is this?
bites.why: Independent of any human use.

bites.q: 'A flower is valuable as a nectar source for pollinating bees.' Which value?
bites.why: Valued as a means to an end.

bites.title: From new dawn to new standard: citizen science in ecology
bites.html: Group 10's topic. Classic: Silvertown (2009), 'A new dawn for citizen science'. Recent: Fraisl et al. (2022), citizen science in environmental and ecological sciences.

bites.title: Remember these
bites.html:
• Citizen science: members of the public take part in real research, mostly by contributing observations.
  • Volunteer data are biased (easy places and times, a few heavy contributors), so filter for quality and model the observation process (effort, occupancy–detection).
  • eBird collects bird checklists with effort data; GBIF aggregates occurrence records. Volunteers supply 50 %+ of GBIF data.

bites.q: Citizen science is…
options: Members of the public contributing to real research
bites.why: Public participation in scientific research and knowledge production.

bites.title: And these
bites.html:
• Ten Principles of Citizen Science (ECSA, 2015): good practice from genuine science outcomes to feedback, open data, credit and ethics.
  • Haklay's levels: 1 crowdsourcing → 2 distributed intelligence → 3 participatory science → 4 extreme citizen science.
  • Silvertown: modern citizen science is open to all, not a privileged few. Fraisl: it is now a standard method, with quality control and ethics built in.

bites.q: Why must citizen-science data be analysed carefully?
options: They are biased toward easy places and times
bites.why: Filter for quality and model the observation process.

bites.q: Haklay's Level 1, where volunteers only collect data, is…
bites.why: Level 1 of 4.
